meta.title: Who really said "Energy and persistence conquer all things"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Everyone credits Benjamin Franklin, but the exact line is in none of his works. It restates the ancient proverb that steady labor conquers all.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Energy and persistence conquer all things'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Franklin, but absent from his papers. A modern rephrasing of Virgil's proverb, echoing Poor Richard's real maxims on industry.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Universally credited to Franklin and fully in the spirit of Poor Richard’s Almanack, but no primary source pins it: the exact wording appears in none of his published works or letters in the Papers of Benjamin Franklin ↗, and it is not listed among his quotations on Wikiquote ↗.

source.heading: What the record shows

docMeta.dd: None located — not in the Papers of Benjamin Franklin

source.excerpt: Energy and persistence conquer all things.
trail: A full-text search of the Papers of Benjamin Franklin ↗ returns no document containing “energy and persistence conquer all things”; the phrase is likewise absent from Wikiquote’s Franklin page ↗, sourced and misattributed sections alike.
Franklin’s authentic Poor Richard sayings carry the identical idea — e.g. “Diligence overcomes Difficulties, Sloth makes them” (1755) ↗.
The sentiment is far older than Franklin: it restates Virgil’s “Labor omnia vicit improbus” ↗ — steady work conquers all.
Quote databases repeat the Franklin credit but cite no source, e.g. The Quotations Page ↗, which lists only his dates.
source.excerptNote: No Franklin document is known to contain these words. The nearest authentic lines are his own Poor Richard maxims: “Diligence overcomes Difficulties, Sloth makes them” (1755) and “All things are easy to Industry, all things difficult to Sloth” (1734).

source.rightsNote: As a short traditional aphorism — and one echoing a proverb some two millennia old — the line carries no meaningful copyright. The attribution to Franklin, however, is unverified.

author.name: Benjamin Franklin
author.heading: Why the line lands on Franklin
author.bio: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) was a printer, scientist and one of the founding fathers of the United States, best known for Poor Richard’s Almanack and its aphorisms on thrift and industry. His genuine maxims — “Diligence overcomes Difficulties, Sloth makes them” and “All things are easy to Industry, all things difficult to Sloth” — made him the natural magnet for any later saying about the power of hard work. He is not, however, documented anywhere as writing the exact line “Energy and persistence conquer all things.”

cite.sourceCitation: Attributed to Benjamin Franklin; no primary source located. The exact wording does not appear in Leonard W. Labaree et al., eds., The Papers of Benjamin Franklin (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1959– ), as digitized at Founders Online, nor among his quotations on Wikiquote.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared “Franklin” lines online, yet it appears in none of his published works, letters or almanacs.

items.why: Repeated as Franklin’s on Goodreads, BrainyQuote and countless motivational sites, but with no citation. A search of the scholarly corpus — the Papers of Benjamin Franklin ↗ — returns no matching document, and Wikiquote ↗ does not list it among his sourced or even his misattributed quotations.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is genuinely Franklinesque — Poor Richard preached that “Diligence overcomes Difficulties” — but the exact words trace to no Franklin document; they modernize the ancient proverb Labor omnia vincit ↗.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Franklin
lead: Franklin built a personal brand on industry decades before the phrase ‘personal brand’ existed. Poor Richard’s Almanack hammered the same message every year from 1733 to 1758 — that steady effort beats talent and luck — so a punchy modern paraphrase about ‘energy and persistence’ slots naturally under his name.

Because the sentiment is authentically his, the misattribution is easy to forgive and hard to dislodge: readers recognize the idea as Franklin’s and assume the words are too. They are not — they are a 20th-century-flavored rewording of a proverb that runs from Virgil through the English ‘perseverance conquers all things.’
context.pull: “All things are easy to Industry, all things difficult to Sloth.” — Franklin’s actual 1734 line
